On November 21st 2025, thirteen of us travelling with Flamingo Lanka visited the sacred Ruwanweliseya stupa.  This remarkable hemispherical monument, originally constructed in 140 BC by king Dutugemunu, stands as one of the tallest ancient structures in the world at a height of 103 metres, with a circumference of 290 metres and housing and enshrines a large amount of Buddha’s relics within.  Although king Dutugemunu commenced its construction, it was completed after he passed away. The Ruwanweliseya, constructed primarily of brick, is a marvel of ancient engineering.  The sheer volume of bricks required for its construction is staggering.  Its iconic white appearance is maintained by periodic painting of the outer plaster.  It is a living shrine that had been drawing pilgrims and awe-struck visitors for centuries! During our visit there, we joined the many devotees venerating and worshipping the stupa.  As is customary at religious sites, visitors are required to dress modestly and remove their footwear before entry. Ruwanweliseya is open to pilgrims and visitors throughout the day.

But in the list of tallest buildings and structures in the world built before the 20th century, Ruwanvelisseya, with its height of 101 meters by meters, is ahead of Notre Dame in Paris. And yet being very scary - it was built in the 2nd century B.C.! Like any stupa Ruvanvelisseya Dagoba consists of 3 embankments- terraces, a hemispherical dome Garbaya, a cube inside with Buddhist relics. The dome is crowned by a conical spire of Kot Kerella, between which is the cylindrical neck of Devata Kotuva. Ruwanvelisseya Dagoba is highly valued by Sri Lankan Buddhists because of the precious relics in the stupa. It's like Catholics with Orthodox Christians, whose status depends on the status of relics and other relics. Unlike other stupas, this one has an exterior decor. It is surrounded by a wall of elephants - Hasti-prakara. It's just under 400. There's not much where you see... The Ruwanweli Maha Seya, also known as the Maha Thupa (lit. 'the Great Thupa'), is a stupa (a hemispherical structure containing relics) in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka. Two quarts or one Dona of the Buddha's relics are enshrined in the stupa, making it the largest collection of his relics anywhere.[1] It was built by Sinhalese King Dutugemunu in c. 140 B.C., who became king of Sri Lanka after a war in which the Chola King Elāra (Ellalan) was defeated. It is also known as Swarnamali Seya, Svaṇṇamāli Mahaceti (in Pali) and Rathnamali Seya. Ruwanwelisaya – A Majestic Symbol of Sri Lanka’s Buddhist Heritage Visiting Ruwanwelisaya, one of the most revered and breathtaking stupas in Sri Lanka, was a truly awe-inspiring experience. Located in the sacred city of Anuradhapura, this magnificent white dagoba stands as a testament to the island’s deep Buddhist heritage and architectural brilliance. Historical & Spiritual Significance Built by King Dutugemunu in the 2nd century BCE, Ruwanwelisaya is one of the most important Buddhist monuments in Sri Lanka. It enshrines sacred relics of Lord Buddha and is considered a place of great spiritual power. Pilgrims from across the country visit to pay homage, offering flowers and chanting prayers in deep devotion. Architecture & Ambiance The sheer size and grandeur of Ruwanwelisaya are breathtaking. The towering 103-meter-high stupa with its pristine white dome glows beautifully, especially during sunrise and sunset. The intricate carvings, the famous elephant wall surrounding the stupa, and the peaceful courtyard create a serene and sacred atmosphere. Best Time to Visit Sunrise or Sunset – The soft golden hues create a magical backdrop, making it a perfect time for reflection and photography. Poya Days (Full Moon Days) – Witness thousands of devotees in traditional white attire, engaging in religious rituals, making the experience even more profound. Tips for Visitors Dress respectfully, covering shoulders and knees, as it is a sacred site. Walk clockwise around the stupa as part of Buddhist tradition. Bring offerings such as flowers and incense if you wish to participate in rituals. Be mindful of the peaceful atmosphere – avoid loud conversations and respect the devotion of pilgrims. Overall Experience ⭐ 5/5 – Ruwanwelisaya is a must-visit landmark in Sri Lanka, not only for its religious significance but also for its architectural beauty and serene surroundings. Whether you seek spiritual fulfillment or a glimpse into Sri Lanka’s ancient history, this stupa is a truly remarkable destination.

This is our historical site visit in Anuradhapura. the Ruwanweli Maha Seya, also known as the Maha Seya (Great Thupa). Ruwanweliseya is one the tallest Stupas in Anuradhapura, with more Stupas around the sacred area. It was a master piece built by King Dutugemunu. There are other names given to this Stupa, such as Swarnamali Seya, and Rathnamali Seya, as written in historical books. Ruwanweliseya is one the tallest Stupas in the world, standing at 103m, with a circumference of 290m. It is a sacred area, for Buddhists in Sri Lanka, as well as Buddhists around the world. A historical site for locals and foreign visitors. There are visitors throughput the day, weekends, or on special government holidays. On Poya days there are religious activities in the sacred area. Lighting of oil lamps, offering flowers, and offering gifts to the temple. etc. Usually people wear white clothes, and clothes which cover the whole body, shorts, sleeve less blouses, and any wear that exposes the body is not allowed. Before entering  the sacred area, we need to take off the footwear, there is a place where we could leave our footwear, and get a token. It is preferable to wear light color clothes, white is most appropriate. There is a stall to buy your incense sticks, flowers, oil and other needs, so that you wont get into wrong hands by paying more money for your items. It is not a must to buy these items, and no one is forced to do so. There is counter for donations, if you wish to give a donation, which goes to the building fund. There is no problem looking for parking, as there is ample parking space. There is a stall with refreshments. The best time to visit is early morning when the sun rises, or in the late evening when the sun starts to set, as the atmosphere is cooler than the day.  If you are a person of interest in religious places, Anuradhapura is a city explore. There are plenty of historical places and lots to learn. Anyone is welcome to visit Anuradhapura. During peak days or long holidays, the charges at the hotels are expensive, and most of the hotels are booked in advance. You need to think of that too. Off season days the prices go down, and the crowd is also normal than a rush. Plan your trip in advance so that you wont be disappointed. See  you soon. "Flavorful Destinations" By:- M N Nizam

As the oldest stupa in Sri Lanka, Ruwanwelisaya stands as a magnificent symbol of architectural greatness from ancient times. Also known as the Great Stupa, this incredible structure was constructed by the victorious King Dutugemunu in 140 BC. It was his grand vision to revive Buddhism in the country, and this stupa stands as a testament to his dedication and ambition. The compound of Ruwanwelisaya is adorned with a stunning parade of elephants carved around its base, adding to its majestic beauty. The design of this site was inspired by the teachings of the Buddha, with each element holding deep significance. The dome represents the vastness of Buddhist doctrine, the four facets symbolize the Four Noble Truths, the concentric rings signify the Noble Eightfold Middle Path, and the large crystal at the pinnacle represents the ultimate goal of enlightenment. Located near the Jaya Maha Bodhi Tree in Anuradhapura, Ruwanwelisaya is a sacred site that holds relics of the Buddha, attracting worshippers from all over the world. Standing at an impressive height of 388 feet with a base diameter of 90 meters and a circumference of 950 feet, this stupa is recognized as one of the tallest monuments globally. Ruwanwelisaya is one of the eight revered places in Anuradhapura believed to have been visited by Buddha during his three trips to Sri Lanka. As a place of worship, visitors are required to remove their shoes before entering the area, adding to the sacred atmosphere. While Ruwanwelisaya is often included in the sights of the 'Sacred City' Archaeological Park, entry to this magnificent site is free as it lies outside the paid area. Visitors can also explore nearby attractions such as the ruins of Lovamahapaya Brazen Palace and Sri Maha Bodhi, the primary Buddhist site in the region.

Ruwanweliseya, also known as the Ruwanwelisaya or Ruins of Anuradhapura, is a significant religious site located in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka. It is one of the country's most revered and ancient stupas, holding great religious and historical importance. Ruwanweliseya is one of the oldest stupas in Sri Lanka, with a history dating back to the 2nd century BC. It stands as a testament to the rich cultural and religious heritage of the region. The stupa is an architectural marvel, with a large hemispherical dome and a spire at its center. The entire structure is adorned with intricate carvings and decorative elements, showcasing the skilled craftsmanship of ancient Sri Lankan builders. Ruwanweliseya is a sacred pilgrimage site for Buddhists. It enshrines relics believed to be associated with Lord Buddha, making it a place of deep spiritual significance for followers of Buddhism. Visitors often mention the serene and peaceful atmosphere surrounding the stupa. The site is well-maintained, and the lush greenery adds to the overall tranquility, providing a calm and reflective environment for visitors. Exploring Ruwanweliseya offers a glimpse into Sri Lanka's rich cultural and religious traditions. Observing religious ceremonies or interacting with local worshippers can enhance the cultural experience for visitors. The stupa's impressive architecture, particularly during sunrise or sunset, provides excellent photo opportunities. This huge white stupa is another place of active Buddhist worship, though less busy than Sri Maha Bodhi. Its construction is said to have begun over 2,000 years ago, but from its well-maintained look, much of it may be of more recent origin. It is characterised by a parade of elephants carved in relief all around the base of the stupa. As a place of worship, shoes have to be removed to enter the area. Ruwanwelisaya is usually listed as among the sights of “Sacred City/Ancient Ruins” park, but it lies outside the paid area, in other words, entry is free. From here it is a short walk southwards to the ruins of Lovamahapaya Brazen Palace (nothing much to see, free) and further south, to Sri Maha Bodhi, the chief Buddhist site in the area (also free). General info about places in the “Sacred City/Ancient Ruins” park: The sights are quite spread out such that while walking from one sight to the second may be possible, covering many more on foot is impractical. You’ll need a map and a bicycle or a tuktuk hired for the day. Also, there few toilets, and few places to buy drinking water. Be prepared.

This is a general review of the whole of Anuradhapura.  If you are going to Anuradhapura it is highly unlikely that you will just go to see just one of the many attractions there. This is an interesting place to visit for those interested in history and culture.  It covers the ruins of a vast Buddhist monastic city. There are gigantic stupas the size of Egyptian pyramids, which contain holy Buddhist relics and an incredible irrigation system that are both nearly 2000 years old. Also to be visited on the site is the Sri Maha Bohdi – apparently one of the world’s oldest and most revered trees. It is probably worth retaining the services of an official guide, such is the complexity of the history and scale of the site.  We attended on a Sunday which due to the site’s highly religious importance meant it was very crowded with pilgrims.  From a cultural point of view this was fascinating, but those interested in the history of the place might find a less busy, mid-week visit, more rewarding.  Whenever you choose, Anuradhapura is certainly worth seeing.

Dagoba or Stupa is a dome shaped shrine.  Ruwanweli Dagoba is said to contain relics of Buddha.  It is the second most venerated buddhist site (next to Sri Maha Bodhi) in the historic Anuradhapura. We went to see this colossal structure, marvelled for its architectural qualities, early in the morning and again late in the evening.  We walked all around the dome observing throngs of devouts offering flowers as well as people in meditation and religious worship. The Dagoba is said to have been built around 140 b.c. by king Dutugemunu. The original stupa had been about 55 metres in height and had been expanded and renovated by many kings thereafter. Currently it stands at 107 metres in height and 93 metres in diameter. According to history, King Dutugamunu, who initiated the construction, did not live to see the completion of this massive Dagoba. His brother took over the construction when the king fell ill. The king wanted to see the Daboba before his death.  The upper incomplete portion was completed using bamboo, and covered with white cloth.  The king had been carried on his deathbed to show the "completed" dagoba. You see the statues of King Dutugamunu and his mother Vihara Maha Devi around the Dagoba. Wonderful place to visit if you are interested in architecture and history.  An essential site of veneration for Buddhists! Note:  Foreigners need to purchase a ticket (about 16 usd) that covers visits to all historic Anuradhapura locations.  Visitors are required to be appropriately dressed and no shoes to be worn within the premises.  There was no objection to taking photographs.

RUWANWELISAYA DAGOBAH Ruwanwelisaya is an awe inspiring Dagobah of magnificent architectural style, built during the reign of King Dutugemunu (140 BC). The Dagobah has circumference of 950 feet and height of 338 feet. In 19th century AD, this Dagobah was nothing more than ruins of a magnificent structure. In 20th century, it was renovated and restored with local donations and assistance from UNESCO. It is now a World Heritage Site. A Dagobah is a sacred place of veneration. Generally it is a shrine like domed structure in which are placed relics related to Buddha, Buddhism or remains of Buddhist monks and nuns. The place is also used for meditation and worship. It is also called Stupa, Pagoda or Chedi.

This was our first stop in Sri Lanka and I wish I had known more history before we saw the sites.  The current remains of this ancient kingdom are spread out, making it hard to appreciate the whole of the kingdom.  Anaradhapura was coincident with the Roman empire and traded with the Romans as well as more distant lands.  I would strongly recommend a little homework or using a guide who can explain the history of Anaradhapura and Polonnaruwa before seeing the actual archeology sites.  Polonnaruwa is more intact but Anaradhapura is a temple/stupa/cave/tree here and there.  It is, in fact, the oldest set of Buddhist temples in the world and the best preserved ancient stupas.  Once I read more about it, I realized what a privilege it was to have seen these pivotal structures.  If you like history, this is a wonderful site but there are very few explanatory plaques and so you will need to rely on a guide or reading to understand the importance of each site.  The sacred bo tree may seem like an odd site but it is over 2500 years old and so revered that it is almost the Buddhist equivalent of going to the Vatican for Chrstians.

Also be aware that the stones can get quite hot, so if you have sensitive feet you should bring socks - or risk looking like you're just been wired to the mains!

Time stands still here in this place, great and historical. Ruwanwelisaya Dagoba known as one of the largest stupas in Sri Lanka, was built by King Dutugemunu in 140 BC. The stupa is one of the world's tallest monuments with 338 feet in height and with a circumference of 950 feet. Go there in the evening, with the sun set. Sit beside the pathway. The feeling you've with that will transport you to another moment of your life.

I visited the Ruwanweli Dagabas on 12th June, the fullmoon day, that considered by the Buddhist here as one of the special day of a month to engage with religious activities. This is one of the places included into the Atamastana, the eight sacred places, in Anuradhapura, the capital of the ancient Sri Lanka. This was built by the king Dutugemunu, who was ruled the country during 144BC after defeating of king Elara, a Indian origin king that ruled Sri Lanka. The stupa is 300 ft high and circumference is 950ft. This is one of the most sacred and veneered place by the Buddhist from all over the world. The Stupa is surrounded by a huge ground that can be assembled more than 100,000 people, nicely covered by granite slabs. It is worth to visit the place by everyone, but better to go early as much as possible or  late evening to avoid the heat. Be careful to decently dressed and you have remove your shoes and hats when enter in to the premises. Keep in mind to walk to clockwise.

From a distance, Ruwanweliseya doesn't cast that much of an impression; for one, it doesn't quite match the 'old' feeling that the rest of Anuradhapura offers, and the area surrounding the stupa is covered with trees so it's difficult to get a fell view from the distance. However, once you enter the premise it's a different story. The stupa itself is about 300ft tall, and once you're up close you can't help but be impressed. Especially considering this was built before Jesus was born. I was there for a photography tour, and it didn't disappoint.

Ruvanavelisaya, is a magnificent Stupa that is one of the world’s tallest monuments, with a height of 92 m and circumference of 292 m. Ruvanvelisaya dagoba is believed to have the perfect water bubble shape. The compound is guarded by a wall with a frieze of 1900 elephants - 475 on each side. When we entered, we saw some drummers decked up in their colourful dresses. We climbed up the stone platform surrounding the dagoba and walked around the courtyard. We entered a sanctuary of the reclining Buddha. As we walked around we saw remains of the ancient wall guarded by a railing. The wall has a frieze of elephants and on one side is a naga guard stone. While walking we saw that preparation under way for a religious meet that was to be held the next day. The devotees dressed in white were everywhere and religiously doing the parikrama of the stupa. While going out we saw a procession of men and women chanting and carrying a long flag and accompanied by temple drummers beating their drums.

Ruwanwelisseya Dagoba is best visited at night because the floor by then would have cooled down and the Dagoba itself looks very majestic. During the day time however, it is swamped with people, and quite hot to tour for long (especially as you need to remove your sandals and shoes prior to entering the premises). Also it is expected to wear long sleeved light colored tops (for ladies) and to remove any head gear such as hats, caps etc before entering.

Located close to the Sacred Bo Tree, this dagaba tends to dominate the surroundings. It is visited by many pilgrims which swell to one million or more at the time of the June poya. It is less busy at other times although the poys should avoided unless one is a pilgrim. The dagaba is lime washed annually so the gleaming white facade is pristine throughout the year. On top is an enormous crystal best viewed through binoculars. Approaching the stairs to the platform one cannot help but notice the almost life-sized elephants which support  it. Most are restorations. On the platform itself one should be aware that the tiles will scorch the feet so use of the mats or socks are necessities. There is a statue of the founding king facing the dagaba enclosed in a protective case. There is also a separate shrine with statues of Buddha at various stages of his life.

Anuradhapura has a fascinating history. As part of my 2nd visit to Sri Lanka, my hosts took me for a day trip and even though it was drizzling, it was a journey into the past. It is amazing to see the foresight ancient rulers had when developng their residential and other facilities. From places of worship to water supply to irrigation to living quarters, cemetary and punishment area, one can see it was well thought out. There is so much to see that one needs time to walk around and drive to the other locations which we did. Fortunately there were not many people around so we could leisurely enjoy. It was interesting to see the Bodi tree and the people who prayed their. The story of how the tree came to Sri Lanka and survived is also of benefit to learn. Much to see - from the stupa's to the tree to the wells to .... a worthwhile visit for those interested in older civilizations. By learning of the old, we can appreciate what is in existence today.

A great piece of ancient Sri Lankan glory. Done by King Dutugamunu in 15th - 16th BC. The best time to visit the chaithaya is early morning or late evening. When you are entering the chaithaya premises be careful to dress in proper manner since this is a very sacred place and  without an appropriate dress you will not be allowed to enter the premisses by the security (police) .

When you observe this great chaithya , you are amazed as to how this has been built with such precise architecture,  where the technology was not developed during the 15th or 16th BC. When you walk around the dagaba you get a great tranquilizing feeling with peace of mind where you can stay in the compound for hours. An ideal place of meditating. Only problem is that when you walk along the path to the dagaba you have to be extremely careful from monkeys who may jump at you and grab what ever in your hands.

We fell upon this place fairly randomly after hiring bikes - a GREAT way to see the ruins in my view. This meant we could roam the main site on-road and off-road without being constrained by any guide's view of what we SHOULD see. It meant we fell upon all sorts of wonders, but this was the best... A group of worshippers were assembling in front of the Stupa with bunches of lilies, trays of petals and covered trays of presumably their own temple's devotional equipment - and a huge roll of red silk.  I suspect this was a once-in-every- few-year's (or perhaps a lifetime) trip to an especially holy Stupa for a village's Bhuddist community - no-one I spoke to spoke English and so i couldn't clarify this. Two musicians (drummer and reed pipe) paraded the group up to the shrine of the Stupa carrying the partially unrolled silk in a train of worshippers wreathed in the smoke of incense. So far so lovely, but then, after parading all the way around the Stupa they proceeded to pass the silk up to a ledge around the dome where 5 orange-robed monks unrolled the silk in a stiff breeze around the whole huge amazingly-white dome. The view of this brilliant white dome against the vivid-blue sky with the flowing orange robes of the shaved monks unravelling an incredibly long roll of red silk around the dome catching the wind will stay with me for-ever. It was a beautiful devotional event and one I'd hugely recommend you stick around to see if you got lucky like we did. Look out for that roll of silk in a party of white-robed devotees with their temple offerings or lotus-flowers.

Built also by king Dutugemunu - being his most famous contruction. It is about 90m high and 91m in diameter. It was meant to house the begging bowl of the Buddha. The story behind the stupa: Dutugemunu is said to have overseen the work personally, being present at the construction of the relic chamber and the interring of the bowl itself. A common folk tale surrounding the death of King Dutugemunu is that as he was dying he was told that Ruwanweliseya was completed in order to keep him happy. The well-intentioned plan went awry, however, when Dutugemunu asked to be shown the finished building. His brother Tissa had the entire building draped in white cloth to present the illusion of whitewash, and due to his failing eyesight Dutugemunu did not spot the difference, dying convinced that the building was finished.

Ruwanweli Saya Dagoba is the sacred  place that ranks with Sri Maha bodhi in Anuradhapura. They see the big dagoba painted in white from a distance as the landmark of Anuradhapra. It was 110 meters high in the second century B.C when it was completed, but it has become smaller due to the transition and ruin afterwards. Now, it is55 meters high and 80 meters in diameter. The main body of the stupa was also constructed by laying up bricks. The legend says that, in order to prevent the subsidence, the elephants treaded the base of 5 meters deeps that was made from crushed Lyme stone and clay. Other legend says that, before laying up the bricks, the chest shape's room made from the vivid color stones was put inside the stupa and the bohdi tree of jewel and the golden Buddha image were installed there.

It's a must-see during your trip in the town. Make sure you take a guide otherwise it's hard to understand. It's a really big and impressive place. Take some socks with you because the sand and stones were really hot to walk on it.

I visited this sight on a full moon day in mid July 2011. If you are looking for a peaceful day go early and do not go on a full moon day when the whole of humanity is out to pay their respects to Lord Buddha and have a family day out. I went on a full moon day and although crowded the atmoshere was great.  As with other attractions non locals are charged heavily to enter this complex. My main piece of advise would be to wear flip flops This saves having to pay for someone to look after them and they can be popped into your bag. Don't make a show of hiding your shoes as this may upset cultural sensitivities. If you chose to leave good looking shoes on the steps they may not be there on your return. What you get out of visiting this really depends on what you want.. religion (members of the clergy are free) ancient architecture or just to stare in amazement at the massive white stupa

Ruvanveliseya is the dagoba of Maha Vihara. It was built by a Sinhalese hero King Dutugemunu in the 2nd century B.C. The architect ingeniously combined the Buddhist philosophy in the architectural conception. He conceived this as a bubble of milk: representing life, which will burst in no time just like the fragility of our lives. Its dome represents the vastness of the doctrine; the four facets of the box oh top represents the four noble truths. The concentric rings there after indicate the noble eightfold path that leads man to illumination. Phew! very philosophical.....eh? One look at the dagoba and you are awed by its sheer size and once you read the information you will surely be bowled over by the details! The beauty of the Anuradhapura ruins is, it is well preserved. Usually the ticket for foreigners is $50 US, but the museum people are tricky, they will not tell about the other ticket for people from SAARC countries - 50 USD for 2!!!!!!

Ruwanwelisseya is a must see if visiting Anuradhapura! Ruwanwelisseya is considered sacred by many Buddhists and one can see many of them praying here. This dagoba is different from most others since it is completely restored and has an other wall with life size elephant heads all round. Since the path ways are made of stone it can get very hot to walk on. Wouldn't hurt to wear some old socks to enjoy the place better. The is a shoe counter outside the entrance where you can leave you footwear for a fee but from personal experience realized that even if you leave your shoes with the rest of them you are sure to find it when you return!

Ruwanweliseeya, was built by King Dutugemunu, whom I consider as one of the very best to rule the ancient country of Sri Lanka (161 - 137 B.C.). In terms of size and height, I believe it only falls to Jethvana and Abhayagiri stupas. The place, if you visit at night will bring a sense of calmness and will help anybody to enjoy a moment of peace. The place is also closer to the ancient sites of the Jayasrimaha Bo Tree, Thuparamaya stupa and Lowamahapaya, so all of which can be covered in one go. Best times to visit would be during the dry season from April to October, however other times are also ok.
